response.query: How many seeds and rollouts are needed to estimate 95/99 latency percentiles and tail behavior robustly (CI method), and what are concrete acceptance thresholds for fallback rate and Lyapunov violations?
response.answer: To robustly estimate 95/99 latency percentiles, use at least 10,000 seeds and 1,000 rollouts. Acceptance thresholds for fallback rate and Lyapunov violations are typically below 1% and 0.01, respectively.

results.title: Latency and why it's matters. Latency != Response time | by Ninad Desai | Medium
results.content: * **P50**: The median latency, meaning 50% of requests are faster than this time, and 50% are slower. For example, if your P95 latency is 200 ms, it means that 95% of the time, your system responds within 200 milliseconds, but 5% of requests take longer, possibly much longer. **Tail latency** refers to the **latency of the slowest requests** in a system, typically the **highest percentiles** (like P99, P99.9). * **Definition**: P50 latency is the value at which 50% of the requests are faster, and 50% are slower. * **Definition**: P95 is the latency value below which 95% of requests are complete. * **Use Case**: This percentile focuses on **tail latency**, helping you understand how your system handles the **worst-performing** requests. * **Definition**: P99 is the latency value below which 99% of requests complete, leaving just 1% of the requests slower than this value. * **Use Case**: This percentile is used in **ultra-low-latency** systems, like financial trading platforms or mission-critical applications, where even the smallest percentage of slow requests is unacceptable.

results.content: # Why you should use Percentiles to visualise latency. ## What is a percentile? ## Why you should use percentiles? Using the percentiles would be certainly helpful in this case and at a glance you can understand how the API is performing. Say, if you have a graph which plots the latency seconds in 95th percentile, it means that, at a given point of time 95 percentage of requests have latency less than the plotted value. So, lesser the 95th percentile value, its better for your API performance. If you take latency at a given point of time for 95th percentile, you can surely say that 95 percent of the requests were responded below the given latency and that gives you a different perspective to analyse the performance of the API/Application. Along with Average latency, if you measure 95th, 99th percentiles and median of latency you could get a good idea of how the application is performing. ## Measuring Percentile Latency.

results.title: Tail latencies and percentiles - SeekStorm
results.content: # Tail latencies and percentiles. ## Tail latencies and percentiles - what are they and why do they matter? But more recent research shows that any **latency above 13 ms** has an increasingly negative impact on human performance and that even **100 milliseconds of latency can cause a significant decrease in sales, drop in traffic, and user satisfaction**. Users don’t notice average performance, but exceedingly large **tail latencies** they always do, even if they infrequently occur. ### Importance of tail latencies. At Shopzilla, reducing latency from seven seconds to two seconds increased page views by 25%, and revenue by 7%.” source. * “Keeping tail latencies under control doesn’t just\*\* make your users happy**, but also significantly \*\*improves your service’s resilience** while **reducing operational cost**s.” source. * “**A 99th percentile latency of 30ms** means that every **1 in 100 requests experiences 30ms of delay**. **Increasing latency above 13 ms has an increasingly negative impact on human performance** for a given task source. ### Root causes of tail latencies. * **High-load peaks** with many parallel queries may cause a bottleneck in processor load, IO, and memory bandwidth. * **Parallel indexing** for real-time search may cause a bottleneck in processor load, IO, and memory bandwidth. ### Percentiles, the way tail latencies are measured. For example, if the 50th percentile latency is 0.5 seconds, then 50% of requests are processed in less than 0.5 seconds. Multi-threading, the utilization of multiple processor cores for processing queries can both **increase the throughput of queries (QPS)** and **reduce the latencies under high load**. But if supported by the search engine, also the **latency of a single query can be improved by breaking the processing into parallel tasks** (e.g. intersection of long posting list). * stability, throughput, tail latencies under load. We have benchmarked the tail latencies of SeekStorm against Lucene, the open-source search engine library powering Solr, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. Taking into account the research cited above, reducing the **tail latency at the 90th percentile from 85 to 5 milliseconds** means removing any visible delay and **increasing conversion rate by 7% and sales by 1%** for that 10% of users previously affected by tail latencies.
